title: Rebuilding Credit After Bankruptcy
summary: Gate 1: Status → Gate 2: Accuracy → Gate 3: Readiness
subtitle: Turn a discharge document into a disciplined credit re-entry plan

blocks.text: A bankruptcy discharge certificate is important paperwork, but it does not come with a tiny marching band or an instant 800 credit score.
What it does is more practical: it confirms that a legal stage has ended, except for debts the law does not release.

This workshop starts after discharge. You will confirm your status, protect the papers that prove it, check both credit reports, fix mistakes and build a small credit system that can survive real life. No product can promise a higher score or an approval date. Your advantage is a clear order of steps and records to back it up.
Discharge, credit-report removal and credit recovery run on three different clocks. Do not use one date as if it controls all three.

items.title: “Discharge means every debt is gone and every creditor must stop reporting it immediately.”
items.text: A discharge releases many debts from before the bankruptcy, but the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act leaves some out. How long a report keeps information is a separate question.

You can tell a real recovery step from a costly shortcut before you sign anything.
blocks.detail: You will know which three checks to pass first, so the first offer in your mailbox never sets the terms of your recovery.
blocks.extra: Noah’s story comes next, then Gate 1 starts with proof of your discharge.

sections.title: Noah’s First Credit Offer Was Not a Welcome Basket

blocks.text: Meet Noah
paragraphs: Noah Sinclair is a warehouse dispatcher in Winnipeg. After a job loss and months of short hours, he filed for bankruptcy. Now he has his discharge, and his old car will not survive another winter.
Then an offer lands in his mailbox: fast approval, high fees and an interest rate that looks like it trained for the decathlon. It feels like a shortcut. He puts it down.
He builds a folder instead: his discharge certificate, the trustee’s letters and a list of every debt in the bankruptcy.

Then he pulls both credit reports. One bureau shows an old credit-card balance as past due right now. That card was part of the bankruptcy. He disputes it with copies of his papers, and the bureau fixes it.

He does not rush to apply. He saves a $500 buffer and runs a three-month test: every bill on time, no overdraft, no credit for groceries. Then he picks a secured card, puts one small bill on it and pays it in full each month.
Nine months later, the bankruptcy is still on his file. But his reports are accurate, his balance is low and his budget has room for a car payment.
Another loan offer shows up. Its rate also looks like it trained for the decathlon. Noah does not even open it.

blocks.text: The first win after bankruptcy may be an accurate report, a cash buffer or six clean due dates. A score is only one way to measure readiness.
Why the story concludes well
Noah did not start with a product. He proved his discharge, fixed his file, tested his budget and opened one account he could manage. The story ended with a system, not a magic number.
Three gates turn a discharge certificate into a credit file you can trust.
blocks.detail: You will check status, accuracy and readiness in order, so you never build a plan on a fact you have not confirmed.
blocks.extra: Gate 1 starts next, with the papers that prove your discharge.

sections.title: Gate 1: Confirm That the Legal Stage Is Actually Complete

blocks.text: This course assumes you have received a discharge. Filing for bankruptcy and being discharged are not the same event. If you are not sure, contact the Licensed Insolvency Trustee who handled your estate before you apply for new credit or tell a creditor that everything was released.
Debts that may survive discharge

OSB guidance lists debts that are not released in the usual way. They include support payments, court fines or penalties, debts from fraud and some student loans, when fewer than seven years have passed since you stopped being a student. Other facts can matter too. Confirm your own list with your trustee or qualified legal advice, not a general course summary.
A discharge certificate proves a legal event. Keep it with the trustee’s contact details and the list of debts in your estate.

items.title: “If an account was listed in the bankruptcy, I can discard every related document.”
items.text: You may need those records to fix a report, answer a future lender’s request for documents or show how an account was treated.

blocks.text: IF YOU ARE NOT DISCHARGED
Different rules apply.
OSB states that someone who is not yet discharged may not borrow more than $1,000 without telling the lender about the bankruptcy. Contact your trustee before you borrow.
OSB: Considering bankruptcy

sections.title: Gate 2: Audit Both Reports Line by Line

blocks.text: Equifax and TransUnion keep separate files.
Review both. A fix at one bureau does not prove the other file changed.

items.title: Identity section
items.text: Check names, addresses and other details. Flag anything that could mix your file with someone else’s.

items.title: Bankruptcy entry
items.text: Compare the filing and discharge details with your trustee papers.

items.title: Included accounts
items.text: Check each creditor name, balance, status and date. Make sure any late-payment reporting after the bankruptcy is accurate.

items.title: Surviving obligations
items.text: Separate debts that were not released from debts in the discharge. Ask your trustee if the treatment is unclear.

items.title: Inquiries and unfamiliar accounts
items.text: Look into applications you did not make, and follow the fraud steps if you need to.

items.title: Dispute package
items.text: Use the bureau’s official steps. Attach copies of the report page, proof of discharge and account papers. Keep the originals.

blocks.text: For a first bankruptcy, FCAC says Equifax and TransUnion usually remove the bankruptcy six years after discharge. TransUnion uses seven years in Newfoundland and Labrador, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Quebec. Multiple bankruptcies may stay for 14 years. Check current bureau and provincial rules.

items.title: “Once the bankruptcy entry is correct, every old account line must disappear.”
items.text: The report may keep showing old accounts and statuses for the usual period. The goal is accurate treatment, not removal of accurate information.

sections.title: Gate 3: Pass the Safe-Credit Readiness Test

blocks.text: The safest time to add credit is when the account has a clear job, you understand the cost, and your budget can pay it without using the account for essentials.
Five readiness questions

items.title: ESSENTIALS COVERED
items.text: Are housing, food, utilities, transport, support payments and required debt payments covered?

items.title: STARTER BUFFER
items.text: Do you have a starter emergency buffer, so one small surprise does not go straight back on credit?

items.title: PAID FROM INCOME
items.text: Can you pay the account on time from ordinary income, including any annual fee and security deposit?

items.title: CLEAR, REPORTED TERMS
items.text: Does the lender report to a Canadian credit bureau, and are the fees, rate and cancellation terms clear?

items.title: ABLE TO WAIT
items.text: Can you wait if the product is expensive, confusing or sold with a guaranteed-score claim?

blocks.text: If a secured card is selected

A secured card usually needs a deposit as security. The deposit is not a prepaid balance and does not replace the monthly payment. Put a small recurring charge on it, keep the reported balance low and pay on time. You do not need to carry interest-bearing debt to build payment history.
The security deposit protects the issuer. Your on-time payments build the new record.

items.title: “Carrying a balance proves I can manage debt.”
items.text: You do not need to pay interest to build payment history. On-time payments, careful use and low balances are what count.

blocks.text: A practical 12-month sequence

items.title: MONTHS 1–3
items.text: Confirm your discharge, audit both reports, fix errors and steady your bills.

items.title: MONTHS 4–6
items.text: Build the cash buffer and, if you are ready, manage one low-cost account that reports.

items.title: MONTHS 7–9
items.text: Keep payments clean, review balances and skip unneeded applications.

items.title: MONTHS 10–12
items.text: Review both reports again. If you need a major loan, compare total cost, not just approval.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: You filed but cannot find proof of discharge. Who should you contact first?
items.detail: The Licensed Insolvency Trustee who handled your estate.

items.title: One bureau shows a pre-bankruptcy account as past due right now. What is the next step?
items.detail: Gather the report page, your discharge proof and the account records. Then use that bureau’s official dispute process.

items.title: A secured card needs a deposit. Does the deposit pay the monthly bill?
items.detail: No. The deposit protects the issuer. You still have to pay the card bill.

items.title: A lender guarantees a 100-point score increase for a large fee. What should you do?
items.detail: Walk away. No lender or product can guarantee a specific score increase.

items.title: What matters more than opening several accounts quickly?
items.detail: Accurate reports, protected essentials, on-time payments, low balances and one account you can control.

sections.title: Your Action: Fillable Bankruptcy Re-entry Plan

blocks.text: Use partial references only. Do not write full account numbers, passwords, PINs, SINs or ID numbers.
Rebuilding after bankruptcy starts with proof and accuracy, not a shopping trip for credit.
blocks.detail: Confirm your discharge, know which debts remain, audit both reports, fix errors, steady your cash flow and add only the credit you can manage. Time and clean recent habits do more work than expensive promises.

blocks.text: The best first application may be no application at all. Being ready means you can manage the account, not just get approved for it.

items.title: Bankruptcy
items.text: A legal process for people who cannot pay their debts, run under Canada’s Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act.

items.title: Licensed Insolvency Trustee (LIT)
items.text: A federally regulated professional who can run bankruptcies and consumer proposals.

items.title: Discharge
items.text: The legal release from many debts included in the bankruptcy, with some exceptions.

items.title: Absolute discharge
items.text: A discharge that takes effect with no conditions attached.

items.title: Surplus income
items.text: Income above the OSB standard. It can change what you must pay and how long the bankruptcy lasts.

items.title: Secured credit card
items.text: A credit card backed by a security deposit. You still have to pay the card balance.

items.title: Re-entry plan
items.text: A step-by-step system for keeping papers, fixing reports, steadying cash flow and using credit carefully after discharge.

quiz.question: True or False: “Carrying a balance proves I can manage debt.”

questions: When did you file, when were you discharged, and what paper proves it?
Which debts might not have been released, and who can confirm?
When did you check each report, and what looked wrong first?
After essentials, how much is left each month, and how big is your buffer?
What is the most you can safely handle in fees, balance and number of accounts?
What will you do in months 3, 6, 9 and 12, and what would make you walk away from an offer?
